CausalChain: Tumor hypoxia → HIF-1α activation → Upregulation of ENTPD2 on tumor cells → Conversion of extracellular ATP to 5′ AMP → MDSC accumulation and activation → Suppression of CTL function → Tumor immune evasion; Inhibition of ENTPD2 + PD-1 blockade → Reduction of MDSC-mediated suppression → Restoration of CTL activity → Tumor regression
Hypothesis: In HCC, targeting the hypoxia-driven ENTPD2 pathway in conjunction with PD-1 checkpoint blockade will mitigate MDSC-mediated immunosuppression and reinvigorate CTL responses, thereby improving antitumor efficacy.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, where hypoxia plays a pivotal role. Under hypoxic conditions, hepatoma cells upregulate hypoxia‐inducible factor 1 alpha (HIF-1α) which drives the expression of ectonucleoside triphosphate diphosphohydrolase 2 (ENTPD2). ENTPD2 converts extracellular ATP into 5′ AMP, fostering the recruitment and functional activation of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). These MDSCs further inhibit cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) activity, promoting immune evasion and tumor progression. We hypothesize that pharmacologic inhibition of ENTPD2, when used in combination with PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitors, could disrupt this deleterious cascade, thereby restoring effective CTL responses and enhancing antitumor immunity in HCC.
